## Answer

Similar matrices have the same trace, so

$$x+4=\operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}B=4,$$

which gives $x=0$. They also have the same determinant. At $x=0$, $\det A=-6$, whereas $\det B=-6(5y-4)$; hence $y=1$. Therefore

$$\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3=\operatorname{tr}B=4,\qquad \lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3=\det B=-6,$$

and the requested value is

$$4^2-(-6)=\boxed{22}.$$

## Answer

The equation $A^2+A=0$ implies that every eigenvalue is a root of $t(t+1)$, so the only possible eigenvalues are $0$ and $-1$. Since $A$ is real symmetric, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. The condition $\operatorname{rank}A=3$ gives $\dim\ker A=1$, so $0$ occurs once and $-1$ occurs three times. Hence

$$A\sim\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,-1,0),$$

which is $\boxed{(D)}$.

## Answer

For

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&1\\a&b&a\\1&a&1\end{pmatrix},$$

its characteristic polynomial is

$$\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda\left[\lambda^2-(b+2)\lambda+2b-2a^2\right].$$

The target diagonal matrix has characteristic polynomial $\lambda(\lambda-2)(\lambda-b)$. Equality therefore requires $a=0$. When $a=0$, the matrix $M$ is real symmetric with eigenvalues $0,2,b$, so it is diagonalizable and is similar to $\operatorname{diag}(2,b,0)$ for every real $b$.

Thus the necessary and sufficient condition is $a=0$ with arbitrary $b$, namely $\boxed{(B)}$.

## Answer

Write $B=P^{-1}AP$. Then

$$B^T=P^TA^TP^{-T},\qquad B^{-1}=P^{-1}A^{-1}P,$$

and

$$B+B^{-1}=P^{-1}(A+A^{-1})P.$$

Thus (A), (B), and (D) preserve similarity. In general, $B+B^T$ cannot be obtained from $A+A^T$ by one similarity transformation because the transpose uses $P^T$ rather than $P^{-1}$. Therefore the incorrect conclusion is $\boxed{(C)}$.

## Answer

All three matrices have eigenvalues $2,2,1$. For $A$,

$$\dim\ker(A-2I)=2,$$

so $A$ is diagonalizable and hence $A\sim C$. For $B$, the upper-left $2\times2$ block is a nontrivial Jordan block for eigenvalue $2$, so

$$\dim\ker(B-2I)=1,$$

and $B$ is not diagonalizable. Therefore $B$ is not similar to $C$. The answer is $\boxed{(B)}$.

## Answer

Equality of the characteristic polynomials of $A$ and $B$ gives

$$x=0,\qquad y=-2.$$

At these values, eigenvectors of $A$ for the eigenvalues $-1,2,-2$ may be chosen respectively as

$$p_1=(0,-2,1)^T,\qquad p_2=(0,1,1)^T,\qquad p_3=(-1,0,1)^T.$$

Therefore

$$P=(p_1,p_2,p_3)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\-2&1&0\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det P=3\ne0,$$

and direct multiplication verifies

$$P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(-1,2,-2)=B.$$

## Answer

The characteristic polynomials of both matrices are $(\lambda-2)(\lambda-1)(\lambda+1)$, so both are diagonalizable with the same three distinct eigenvalues and are therefore similar. One solution of $AP=PB$ is

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2&1\\1&-1&0\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Since $\det P=2\ne0$, this matrix is invertible, and direct multiplication gives $P^{-1}AP=B$.

## Answer

A solution of the equivalent equation $AP=PB$ is

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&-1\\1&-2&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its determinant is $-1$, so it is invertible. Direct calculation then verifies

$$P^{-1}AP=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}=B.$$

The eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ are $1,3,-2$, and $\det A=-6$. Hence the corresponding eigenvalues of the adjugate $A^*$ are

$$\frac{-6}{1}=-6,\qquad \frac{-6}{3}=-2,\qquad \frac{-6}{-2}=3.$$

The columns of $P$ are ordered as $\alpha_1,2\alpha_3,-\alpha_2$; nonzero scaling does not change the associated eigenvalue. Therefore

$$P^{-1}A^*P=\operatorname{diag}(-6,3,-2),$$

so the answer is $\boxed{(C)}$.

## Answer

Because $\alpha,\beta$ are unit vectors and $\alpha^T\beta=1/3$,

$$A\alpha=\frac13\alpha+\beta,\qquad A\beta=\alpha+\frac13\beta.$$

Any nonzero vector orthogonal to both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is annihilated by $A$, so $0$ is an eigenvalue. Moreover,

$$A(\alpha+\beta)=\frac43(\alpha+\beta),\qquad A(\alpha-\beta)=-\frac23(\alpha-\beta).$$

Thus $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha-\beta$ are eigenvectors. Together with a nonzero vector in $\operatorname{span}\{\alpha,\beta\}^{\perp}$ they give three linearly independent eigenvectors, corresponding to the distinct eigenvalues $4/3,-2/3,0$. Hence $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix.

## Answer

From $AB=0$, $\operatorname{im}B\subseteq\ker A$, so

$$\operatorname{rank}B\leq n-\operatorname{rank}A.$$

On the other hand, $A+BC=I$ gives

$$n=\operatorname{rank}I\leq\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}(BC)\leq\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B.$$

Combining the two inequalities yields $\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B=n$.

Multiplying $A+BC=I$ on the left by $A$ gives

$$A^2+ABC=A.$$

Since $AB=0$, this reduces to $A^2=A$. The minimal polynomial of $A$ divides $t(t-1)$, which has distinct roots, so $A$ is diagonalizable.
